Species names and the name table

Source: vignettes/articles/species-names.Rmd
species-names.Rmd

The released models were trained on species names in the European Vegetation Archive (EVA) standardized to the World Flora Online (WFO) taxonomic backbone (21 June 2026). A table of new plots names its species as they were entered in the field, by a current accepted name, or by a name from another checklist, and the models read a name only when it is exactly one they learnt. The name table, names.json, maps the names a user may write to the names the models learnt. This article explains where its links come from, which taxonomic backbones it reads, and how a name is matched through it. Reading a table’s names through it during imputation is covered in Imputing new plots; installation in Installing the RESOLVE engine.

Why a name can differ from the model’s name

EVA’s contributing databases enter each species under their own checklist’s name, and EVA standardized every record to WFO. The two need not agree. EVA resolved its 71,014 records entered as Anemone nemorosa to Anemone altaica, so a model knows wood anemone only under that name. A table may also use the accepted name, Anemonoides nemorosa in WFO, and an older table may call pedunculate oak Quercus pedunculata, which WFO lists as a synonym of Quercus robur. Without the table, all three names count as species the model never saw, and their records are left out of the imputation.

How the table is built

Each link in the table maps one name to one token, a name some released model holds in its vocabulary. The links come from two sources, read in order:

  1. EVA’s records. Each name a vascular plant record was entered under is linked to the token most of that name’s records were resolved to. This gives Anemone nemorosa → Anemone altaica.
  2. The synonymy of the taxonomic backbones. In each backbone, every entered name and every token is looked up; its accepted name and all synonyms of that accepted name are linked to the token those records were resolved to. This gives Anemonoides nemorosa → Anemone altaica and Quercus pedunculata → Quercus robur. A backbone spanning several kingdoms is read for plants only.

A name that several sources link to different tokens takes the link from the earliest source (EVA, then the backbones in the order of the table below), then the token with most records. A name that is itself a token is never in the table, so a name a model holds is always read as written. A model renames a name only when its own vocabulary lacks the name and holds the token; the released models differ in vocabulary, so the same table can rename a name for one model and not for another.

The released table holds 299,549 names linked to tokens of the 17,890 species the released models hold between them. For each name it also records which sources agree on its token: 62,492 names are linked by one source alone, the others by two to twelve. For 54,744 names some source links another token; the file keeps those alternatives beside the chosen link (support and alternatives), so a disputed name can be checked.

The taxonomic backbones

The backbones are read through the taxify package, each at the release recorded in names.json. World Flora Online comes first because EVA resolved its records to it.

Order Backbone Release (upstream date) Names whose link it gives Names it links to the same token
1 World Flora Online (WFO) 2026.06 (2026-06-21) 159,032 166,218
2 Euro+Med PlantBase 2026.08 (2026-07-11) 14,613 59,166
3 World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) 2026.06 (2026-06-04) 40,880 181,843
4 Leipzig Catalogue of Vascular Plants (LCVP) 2026.08 (2022-11-07) 27,263 145,072
5 Catalogue of Life (COL) 2026.09 (2026-09-11) 19,914 182,953
6 GBIF Backbone Taxonomy 2023.08 (2023-08-28) 18,347 204,942
7 Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS) 2026.09 (2026-08-27) 2,207 11,532
8 NCBI Taxonomy 2026.09 (2026-09) 710 11,745
9 Open Tree of Life 2026.09 (2025-12-20) 355 3,150
10 Catalogue of Life Extended Release (COL XR) 2026.09 (2026-09-25) 5,084 208,842
11 World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS) 2026.09 (2026-09-01) 284 20,043

The fourth column counts the names whose chosen link came from that backbone; the fifth counts every name the backbone links to the chosen token, whether or not an earlier source gave the link first. EVA’s records give the remaining 10,860 links. The eight other backbones taxify holds (Index Fungorum, AlgaeBase, FishBase, SeaLifeBase, the Reptile Database, the Mammal Diversity Database, AviList and LPSN) were read as well and give no link: they hold no vascular plants, or none that an earlier source had not already linked.

Matching a name through the table

A name is read in steps, and the first that reaches a token wins: as written when the model’s vocabulary holds it (exact), through the table (alias, with the source of the link), as the nearest name within one edit of a token or a table name (spelling, with the name it was read via), and otherwise left as written (unresolved). The example writes a table of three real links in the format of names.json and resolves six names against a vocabulary of two species.

table <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
writeLines('{"source": "example",
  "aliases": {"Anemone nemorosa": ["Anemone altaica", "eva"],
              "Anemonoides nemorosa": ["Anemone altaica", "wfo"],
              "Quercus pedunculata": ["Quercus robur", "wfo"]}}', table)

vocabulary <- c("<UNK>", "Anemone altaica", "Quercus robur")
resolve.names(c("Anemone altaica", "Anemone nemorosa", "Anemonoides nemorosa",
                "Quercus pedunculata", "Quercus robru", "Carex firma"),
              vocabulary, table = table)
#>                   name           token      route source           via distance
#> 1      Anemone altaica Anemone altaica      exact                             0
#> 2     Anemone nemorosa Anemone altaica      alias    eva                      0
#> 3 Anemonoides nemorosa Anemone altaica      alias    wfo                      0
#> 4  Quercus pedunculata   Quercus robur      alias    wfo                      0
#> 5        Quercus robru   Quercus robur   spelling        Quercus robur        1
#> 6          Carex firma     Carex firma unresolved                             0
import json, tempfile
import resolve_core as rc

table = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".json", delete=False, encoding="utf-8")
json.dump({"source": "example",
           "aliases": {"Anemone nemorosa": ["Anemone altaica", "eva"],
                       "Anemonoides nemorosa": ["Anemone altaica", "wfo"],
                       "Quercus pedunculata": ["Quercus robur", "wfo"]}}, table)
table.close()

vocabulary = ["<UNK>", "Anemone altaica", "Quercus robur"]
rc.resolve_names(["Anemone altaica", "Anemone nemorosa", "Anemonoides nemorosa",
                  "Quercus pedunculata", "Quercus robru", "Carex firma"],
                 vocabulary, table=table.name)
#>                    name            token  ...            via distance
#> 0       Anemone altaica  Anemone altaica  ...                       0
#> 1      Anemone nemorosa  Anemone altaica  ...                       0
#> 2  Anemonoides nemorosa  Anemone altaica  ...                       0
#> 3   Quercus pedunculata    Quercus robur  ...                       0
#> 4         Quercus robru    Quercus robur  ...  Quercus robur        1
#> 5           Carex firma      Carex firma  ...                       0
#>
#> [6 rows x 6 columns]

Anemone altaica is the model’s own name. The entered name Anemone nemorosa reaches it through EVA’s records, the accepted name Anemonoides nemorosa and the synonym Quercus pedunculata through WFO. Quercus robru is one edit from Quercus robur. Carex firma is in neither the vocabulary nor the table and stays unresolved; its records would be left out.

The released names.json ships with the models in the Zenodo record of the browser app, inside models.tar. Its path is the table argument of resolve.names() in R and resolve_names() in Python, and the names argument of the loaders and of suite imputation.
